utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters, to the court reporters, to all counsel. We can resume now with the cross-examination of Mr. Jankovic. Is that correct, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Slobodan Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, what do you have, about another 30 minutes that you need? So about 10 minutes to 3.00 is when you should finish. That is so long as the witness comes right into the courtroom. Well, we are not going to count every single minute, you know. I am talking approximately. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jankovic. Please be seated. Let me remind you that you are still under oath and that you are being asked questions by Mr. Cayley from The Office of the Prosecutor, and he'll ask you questions for about a half hour as part of the cross-examination. Mr. Cayley, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Judge Shahabuddeen, good afternoon counsel

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jankovic. I hope you enjoyed a pleasant evening in The Hague last night.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated yesterday that one cannot evaluate the range on the basis of crater analysis. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the reason for that, Professor, is because it is extremely difficult to accurately measure the angle of impact of a shell, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that depends. No, I didn't say that. I mean, if you have the beginnings of a hole where the projectile has gone in, if you have that -- I don't know whether that existed or whether they exploded. I don't know if there was a crater or if there was not, or there was the beginning of a hole, but if there is, on the basis of the access of that hole you can see where the projectile is coming from. That happens frequently. But I don't think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you are stating in this particular case there wasn't a good crater from which to measure the angle of impact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if that was the case and the angle of impact was inaccurately measured, that would vastly change the calculations that you made for the Defence, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we are getting into a technical discussion. Just a moment, please. I said that I never saw the effect on asphalt, and in the text I read, that there were very clear radii on the asphalt, which I didn't see that. You can't see that on the photographs either. However, it is true -- let's make a distinction. What I was talking about yesterday was mathematics, and those were exact things. Now we are talking about opinions. It is probable -- I didn't make that kind of a calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you want to interrupt the witness? Excuse me, Mr. Jankovic, the Defence Counsel wants to say something. I am going to give him the floor for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am afraid, because we are talking about technical terms, that the interpretation from French into English was not technically correct. Mr. Jankovic has been talking about dispersion and also the direction from which the shell is coming, and, to the best of my knowledge, as far as the English language is concerned, my learned colleague, Mr. Cayley, has been asking about the angle of fall, whether it can be calculated properly, and Professor Jankovic is answering about dispersion and about setting the right direction. So these are two different things. Of course, Professor Jankovic understands what I am saying in Croatian, so let us please clarify this matter, because the difference is substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The Prosecutor has a limited amount of time and I don't want him to be interrupted too frequently. He has about 30 minutes. Mr. Cayley, could you reformulate your question. I'll ask you, Mr. Jankovic, even though it is a very technical subject, to try to answer as close to the question as you can. This is for time reasons, and in terms of equity between the Defence and the Prosecution. Thank you very much. Mr. Cayley, would you please reformulate your question and, as much as possible, try to take into account Mr. Nobilo's questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the questions. Perhaps I was making a rather long introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you've understood the question and if you can answer it, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The two things are connected. One cannot answer the questions just by speaking out of the air. It requires a technical analysis and that takes some time. I would have to do some calculations. I would have to look at things. I would have to study things. One cannot give answers just like that, just speaking. But the two things can be connected, one to the other, and I can explain why. But that would take some time, and I don't know -- and it will take time if I were to go into those details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, it's not my time that's being counted here. Mr. Cayley is the one who has to decide about the density of the questions that he is asking. It seems to me that the question he asked was simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I thought so, Mr. President, and in fact the witness answered my question. He was trying to explain that when a shell hits the ground, it makes a radii-like pattern. That was the translation that I got. That's what I understood he was saying. In any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, it is correct, is it not, from the photographs that you saw, that it would have been difficult to accurately measure the angle of impact of the shell on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: On the photographs you can't see anything. No conclusions can be drawn from those photographs. They are absolutely unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if there was an inaccuracy in the angle of impact, that would make your graphs here, frankly, not of very much use to the Court, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, because what I said to you was that I did the calculations on the initial velocity of 735, and I told you that the Croatian army did not have that table, didn't have that charge. However, I presented the results in order to show you that even with those results, the data do not coincide among themselves. They are contradictory. But the most important thing is, I believe, is that the Croatian army did not have those tables and could not use that supercharge. You call that additional charge in your texts. But it was out of the question to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, listen very carefully to my question, because at the moment I am talking about the accuracy of the angle of impact. If there was a 10-degree inaccuracy in the angle of impact when this shell hit the ground, how would that effect the range? Let's say it hit the ground at an angle of 54 degrees, how would that effect the range of this shell?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I gave you the tables and the results. I am not speaking, the results speak for themselves. I can take them out, I can show them to you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no. Excuse me, Mr. Jankovic. If I've understood the question, it's not a question of finding the same results. If I understood the Prosecutor's question, it is, let's say, that there was a 10-degree error, what would the result of that be in respect of the range? The question has to do with the range. I am not sure that the French was correctly translated. I hope it was. It usually is. Is that your question, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's exactly the question, Mr. President. If the witness could be given Exhibit D526, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, Professor, to diagram "I".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO so that the public gallery can see. These are technical questions, we are talking about the shelling of a city, and there were deaths and there were wounded people. It's a tragic situation. We are talking about "I" now, are we not? Yes, "I."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the estimate given by Witness W is 44 degrees. I have asked you if there had been an inaccuracy of 10 degrees in that measurement, whether that would have increased the range. Now, if we look at document "I," we see an impact angle of 53.4 degrees. Can you tell the Court what the range would be had the shell hit the ground at 53.4 degrees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's on the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, be careful with the question, as I heard it translated into French. Be careful. You said 53.4 twice, 53.4. That's what the calculation is that's been done. You were talking about 44, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can call it 9.4 degrees inaccuracy, if you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there had been a 9.4 inaccuracy in the measurement of the angle, this chart would have applied, wouldn't it, Professor, and the range would have been 16.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From this chart, this chart represents the standard OF 462 ammunition with the additional charge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: What's the question? What's the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Chart "I" refers to the trajectory of standard OF 462 Russian-type ammunition with an additional charge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me repeat. Croatia did not have the firing tables, it had the velocity. I did the calculation because in the text that's -- additional charge was what was spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's not mix up things. You are also mixing things. Let's not confuse opinions with technical questions. For the time being you are talking about technical issues. You said, "I don't want to mix opinion with technical issues," so let's not go back to what was said yesterday and see whether or not Croatia had that charge. Please try to answer the question that Mr. Cayley asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, if we could look at diagram "C" now, and this is in connection with the M76 ammunition. Now, had Witness W inaccurately measured the angle of impact by 4 degrees, 4.1 degrees to be precise, this chart would have applied, wouldn't it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The range of the shell would have been 16.000 metres, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, do you know what the maximum range of standard OF 462 ammunition is with a full charge, so not supercharged, with a full charge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I have some tables in my briefcase. I could take them out and then answer exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please go ahead. The maximum range with a full charge and a low elevation on the barrel of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: 15 kilometres, 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the maximum range of the OF 462 ammunition with full charge is 15.300 metres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the testimony that you read that was provided to you by the Defence, have you seen anywhere in that evidence an exact grid reference on a map locating this artillery piece that fired these shells on Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that Witness W said that the weapon was 16.000 metres away from Zenica; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and with me I have the notes indicating the page and on what line this data is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying, Professor, that you faithfully abided by that figure of 16.000 metres, didn't you, in making your calculations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you had read Witness W's testimony very carefully, you would have seen that he stated that, in fact, the weapon was about 16.000 metres away from Zenica; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Page 6.024, lines 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, also 6.029, line 7 and page 6.091, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, Professor, that it stated, and I'll read it for the purposes of the transcript, this is Witness W: "The angle at which the shell landed tells us that the artillery weapon was about 16.000 metres away from the town of Zenica." On page 6.029, I think at lines 7 and 8, Judge Riad asked: "How far is it from Zenica?" "This point, Your Honour, is about 16.000 metres away from Zenica." Is that the transcript that you read, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, for completeness, I think it's absolutely necessary to read the portion of the transcript that puts this in context. On the next page, page 6.025, the witness was asked: "Is it your opinion that the shell also had an additional charge, an additional propellant to cover the extra distance?" Answer: "On the basis of our findings, it was assessed that the gunman had to have used a shell with an additional charge." End of answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're not going to argue about the transcripts. The Judges are capable of reading the transcripts. For the time being, we're listening to Mr. Cayley's cross-examination. When you redirect, Mr. Hayman, you can point out what you want to point out. Let me remind you also that, during the deliberations, the Judges are capable of reading the 17.000 pages of transcript. In fact, that's their jobs and that's their responsibility. Let's not begin to argue right now. We have a technical person here, and the cross-examination is being conducted normally. Mr. Cayley, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that the witness was giving an estimate of the distance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, had you read Major Baggesen's testimony, Professor, you would have found that he stated at page 1.940 that he estimated the range at 14 to 15 kilometres in a westerly direction from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Last night, I read those pages, I received them, and if I understood correctly, he said that the range of the weapon was 14 to 15 kilometres. That's what he said, and he said it on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Everybody agrees. Everybody agrees.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Line 21 of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I did not catch the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The page number was 1.940.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you show me in the models that you've provided to the Court one of these models which actually shows a range of less than 14.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: OF 462, I've got firing tables, and I can answer anything you want to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. What I'm interested in, Professor, is Exhibit 526. Does one of the models that you have demonstrated to the Court show a range of less than 14.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't understand it either, Mr. Cayley. Would you please ask it again? I'm not sure I understood it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, in these tables in D526, you show the possible maximum range of a 122-millimetre shell with a number of variables, including the degree of impact, the target height, and the gun height. Is there any one of these tables where the maximum range of a shell in these particular circumstances is less than 14.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know whether it's 229. I didn't catch the beginning of your question. On the graph that I showed you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can help me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought you were talking about letters. You're talking about 526, Mr. Cayley. We have to be clear here. It's a very technical discussion and very important, we all know that. So that 526 has several letters. Just a moment, Mr. Hayman, I'll try to clarify everything. You'll see. Trust me. D526, which is a Defence Exhibit, has several documents, but they are indicated by letters, Mr. Cayley. Could you tell the witness, and here I agree with the witness, he can't answer, what document are you talking about? Is it K? Is it L?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll direct the witness straight to the document. It's document N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That's clear now, so we're talking about document N. Very well. Document N. It's a chart which shows an OF 462 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the range on this particular table, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: 14 kilometres, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To be exact, 14.220 metres, I think, is your calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that from B, C, F, D, G, I, and N, this is the lowest range of all of the values expressed in these tables?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's move along. Let's move along, Mr. Cayley. That was clear. That was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated to the Court just now that last night you were provided with the testimony of Major Lars Baggesen who estimated the range to be between 14 and 15 kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All of that was said, Mr. Cayley. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, when Major Baggesen was quoted, he said that the range of these 122-calibre weapons is 14.000 to 15.000 metres, but that that was the possible range, not that that was the actual range there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you will have the redirect. Please wait until the end of the cross-examination. Just wait until the end of the cross-examination. You will be able to redirect and make any comments you want. Don't disturb Mr. Cayley in his demonstration. Mr. Cayley, try to get to the essentials. The witness said it to you already. We're talking about 14 kilometres, 222 metres. What is the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo has misrepresented Major Baggesen's testimony, but I will move on as you're requesting, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, what do you know about the characteristics of the D130J weapon. Are you familiar with its handling characteristics? I'm sorry, the D30J. I've just said "D130."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking the characteristics of the weapon, not of the projectile, that is, the 30J that you're talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct, the weapon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The gun.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Without the documentation, it's difficult to speak, but ask me what you want. If I can answer it, I will, if not, well, then I can't. I can only add, if it's of interest for you, it's my father who built it. He built the Yugoslav version. Therefore, ever since I was a child, I've been familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I hope that in your childhood you were given other toys, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were little guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, it's not assumed that because daddy is familiar with the gun, the son is familiar with the gun as well. Ask your question again, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Professor, the D30J is a highly mobile weapon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's known for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It can be towed behind a vehicle, can it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's very easy, isn't it, to move it 1.000 or 2.000 metres backwards or forwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's relative when you say "easy." "Easy" is relative. You know, that's just relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It can be set up quickly to use in action, can't it, as a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how much time it takes to move a weapon. I couldn't tell you that. That's not a technical problem. You'd have to ask military people about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it be quicker to set up a 122-millimetre D30J for action than, for example, a 155-millimetre howitzer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said to you that I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're getting into hypotheses now, Mr. Cayley. We can't ask the witness to invent scenarios. He's an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I showed you a video of a D30J, would you be able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the lights could be brought down, please, and the video played. Just to introduce this video, this is a video actually involving Mr. Ivica Rajic and a shelling incident from Kiseljak, but it does very graphically represent the artillery piece which we're discussing within the accused's area of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Watch very carefully, Professor. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo? Mr. Cayley, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My colleague is not receiving any interpretation of this text. We don't know when this was recorded and what this man is saying, my colleague doesn't and the Judges don't, which is most important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought that that was not important. I thought that's not what the important thing was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's not, Mr. President. I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have a copy for Mr. Hayman, if he wants what is stated put into evidence. It is the gun that is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't know what the date of the tape is, we don't know where the tape was made, and we're told we can't listen to it and understand what the person is saying to try and date it or put it in a place or a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the problem, Mr. Hayman. The problem is that the Prosecution wants to show you the picture of a gun. We haven't seen the gun yet. What the person is saying, for the time being, for the time being, is not very important. If you don't mind, let the video be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, the Prosecutor said this photo, this videotape, will place this gun under the command and control of my client. That is what he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, let me remind you there is somebody here who is directing the discussion, that is, Judge Jorda with Judge Shahabuddeen. I just said that the videocasette was going to be shown. You will have it. The Prosecution said that it was showing it to show a gun, and you can make your objections when you redirect. Time is running for the Prosecution. Let me direct things here. Don't you think that I also have a certain amount of possibility to direct things and some authority here? Don't you think we're wasting a lot of time? I'm the accountant of the time, if you like, here, as you are. Let the Prosecution conduct its cross-examination. Don't force me, once again, to intervene, and once a decision has been taken by the Judges, I will ask the parties to comply with it. Mr. Cayley, please proceed. We will show the video. The Judges don't need it for the time being. It's the Judges who decide things here. Mr. Cayley, continue with the video and show us the gun. I can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will provide a copy of the videotape to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You will get a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the video could be continued, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's continue. Yes, please be seated. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is the important part of the news report. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Now, the question, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the picture can be paused, please. Sorry, can the picture be placed back on the screen? Could the picture of the artillery be placed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you recognise it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the fundamental point of the question that Mr. Cayley is asking. Mr. Jankovic, do you recognise the weapon as the Prosecutor has referred to it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recognise it. In order to see whether it has the characteristics for the 122 shell, we see the large plate on which everything turns. You can't really see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would you recognise it if you saw the double-baffled muzzle brace? It probably won't be translated. The tip of the barrel of the gun is distinctive on a D30J, is it not, Professor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is the end of the barrel of a D30J distinctive, the baffle?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the muzzle where the ring is that you use in order to fire? I think I saw that. Well, it could be on the other guns also. Listen, these kinds of things are things that journalists recognise. We technicians, we work with technical data, not with pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I've almost finished, Professor. You stated yesterday that Croatia does not have, and indeed you have never seen, range tables for M76 ammunition. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How were you able to use M76 ammunition from 1996 onwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't use it. I didn't understand the question. Are you asking whether I use it today? Well, no, I didn't use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's an ambiguous question, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you don't have the range tables for a particular piece of ammunition, you can't use that ammunition in an artillery piece, can you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you stated that Croatia has never had the range tables for M76 ammunition. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to know that Croatia has been advertising both its 122-millimetre howitzer and M76 ammunition for sale since 1996?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How is it --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In Abu Dhabi we provided a brochure about that projector, but without the firing tables. We considered if we could sell it, at that point we could draw up the firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How is a country able to use ammunition that you are selling without range tables?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the country doesn't do it. It was a company that made the offer. I said that we had the documentation and that we could produce it, and if anybody wants to buy it, at that point we can produce it. I said that now we have the range tables and the possibility of establishing those tables, and we can do it. Let me add again that now we are not interested in that because we have much better projectiles. The one that I had built is much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, lastly, you state that after the war began the Croatian government asked you to become a technician in an institute in Zagreb. What was that institute that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The name in Croatian is Brodaski Institute. That is the institute for ships, ship construction industry, and I worked there until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have any sort of military rank prior to retirement from your service in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, after my studies in Brussels, I was an officer in that army, and that was until 1962. I left -- '72. I was a Lieutenant-Colonel, I was a Colonel, but then I decided that I wanted a scientific career, not a military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Let me now turn to the Defence. It is with pleasure now that I give you the floor, and you can use this time as you like, Mr. Nobilo. I hope that the Prosecution is not going to interrupt you as much as you interrupted it. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try and be more correct in posing my questions. Professor, could you tell us whether you would be able, had you been in Zenica on that unfortunate day, to calculate the angle of fall of the projectile, the one where it hits the ground, that angle? Would you have been able to calculate that had you been in Zenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that's not so easy. To answer in principle is difficult. I can tell you what I would have done had I been there. In any case, what surprised me the most is that I would analyse all of the impact sites, not just one, and that way, if I were to get any kind of result, I would have all the results and I would be able to make comparisons and conclude what the average is and what's the dispersion, what is the plausible gap between the results in order to do that study correctly. That's how I would answer, a priori, a posteriori. I can't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness W and Major Baggesen, how many craters did they look at, if you recall by reading through the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood the material correctly, it was based on one. At times they speak about the other impacts here and there, that it fell here or fell there, but I had the impression that the conclusions were drawn from a single impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Professor, am I right in saying that from the shell and from the crater you are trying to determine the angle of fall, that is one element, but that witnesses tried to determine and calculate from the crater, to determine from the crater the direction from which the shell was launched --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am objecting at this point. That is a matter that was never addressed, the bearing, the bearing of fire was never addressed in the examination-in-chief or in the cross-examination. The angle of impact and the direction of fire are two distinct matters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I think that the questions are so technical, and we are fortunate to have a technical expert here. All right. Continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The questions intermingle. Could you tell the Court, please, first, whether it is easier to look at the crater and by its aspect to determine the angle of fall, or the bearing of fire, that is to say the direction from which the shell came? What's easier?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeated that I had a lot of craters on the earth, but not on asphalt. On firing ranges, it's almost impossible to say from where and what the angle of fall is of the projectile. It is true that one can apply information using fragments, that is the -- they call it the axe effect, that the walls of the shell disperse and they fly all around the projectile. It's true that the -- it's usually that the rocket remains in one piece and that the base remains in one piece. Ordinarily, we recognise from what projectile is involved by the large pieces, but when we fire projectiles, ordinarily the base is also found in one piece or split into two, so one can recognise what is involved. But we never tried to go in the other direction, that is using the crater as a starting point in order to know what is the bearing or the angle. I never saw that done. I haven't done any kind of work on that subject to see whether anyone has done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Professor, in the literature anywhere in the world, have you ever come across the fact that the caliber, the range from which it was shot and the bearing is determined on the basis of a crater without any instruments, just by looking at it and with a compass? Have you ever come across that in the literature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never saw that and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the caliber is determined according to the traces of the shell. Could you explain to the Court what, as a rule, is found, what parts are usually found, and how do you know what caliber was used, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that the walls whose pieces, pieces of different sizes, and ordinarily it's very important to know the size of the piece from a shell. That's why special tests are carried out. The shell is put into sand, into a closed space, you measure the curve of the dispersion of the large pieces. Eighty per cent of the weight of the projectile are pieces that can be said to be large. That's very important to know, because that tells us what the effects of the different pieces are. As I also said, ordinarily the rocket remains in one piece, it's found on the ground, and as well as the base, because it's very thick. It always remains in one piece or almost in one piece, perhaps broken into two pieces, but they were large pieces that can be recognised. The other pieces are very dispersed, that is those of different sizes, and I said that it's very interesting, and we always look at -- there are special tests. We look for the dispersion of the pieces to see what is the percentage of the pieces that are large and those that are small, and there's a specific diagram for each projectile. Somewhere in the text I found that they were pieces that were larger or smaller than this caliber should be, which is not impossible. It's impossible to find for all sizes in one single caliber and to take what you want. They say this is a smaller one, this is a bigger one, this is another big one, another small one, but you can't go the other way, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that on the basis of these pieces you cannot determine this. How can you determine in the most certain terms caliber? You mentioned the base of a shell. Perhaps I didn't receive the translation, but the fuse, is the fuse usually on the spot?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, after the explosion, ordinarily, I am not saying always, but ordinarily, in most cases the rocket remains almost in one piece and the base is in one piece or broken into two or three pieces. And therefore the rocket, when it's in one piece, even if -- on the rocket -- because it's indicated on the rocket what it is. That's how we know what it is. On site we know that it's the crater produced by this projector because there were a lot of craters on site. That's the first thing. But when you find the pieces of the base, that is the back part which is very thick and which doesn't break --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, Professor. For the transcript, your expression Upaljac was translated as rocket -- no fuse. Was that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat this in the different languages. Upaljac in French is la fuseer. In English it's the fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you spoke about fuse, not rocket, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, here we are not talking about rockets, no. We shouldn't say rockets. It's the fuse. In French it's la fuseer and in English it's fuse. It's baza in Croatian and then base in English and French culot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think the interpreters appreciate the various possibilities. These are technical terms. I am trying to help them. We can continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I should like to mention that it was the error of the Defence for not giving the interpreters a list of terms. It is difficult for them to know in advance the different areas and technical terminology that we use, so the Defence Counsel would like to apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the scene itself, according to the report on the spot, made on the spot by the judge, a fuse was found. It was 152 millimetres. Did you see that fact in the material, I mean, that we gave you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember, they speak about the fuse and about 155, 152. I am not sure if they speak about 150. But I said yesterday, and I can repeat it today, that a projectile, a fuse, is used on several projectiles, and that's characteristic here. That is the fuse RGM2 is used, it is a Russian fuse. There is also the former Yugoslav version, which is UTUI. And that fuse is used as 122, 130 and 152 millimetres, the three completely different projectiles and three completely different systems, but it's the same fuse. So one has to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have almost completed. Defence Exhibit 230, you have seen that diagram, have you not? Can you tell us, it was the Prosecutor's exhibit, is this trajectory mathematically correct? We can place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is exact mathematically speaking. The mathematics, what I showed you, and anyone can make the comparisons in order to see what the comparison is. Now, as much as I can see just like this, that it doesn't correspond, if I look at things quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I would need some time in order to know exactly, in order to say this is not quite right, it should be this or it should be that. I would have to look at all of the comparisons and all of the -- but that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we say it isn't necessary, is this the exhibit -- the exhibit was provided by whom? It was the Prosecution case, given during the Major's testimony? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was Witness W who spoke at greatest length on the shelling of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleague for a moment. The Judges are going to decide that after the questions they want to ask, and after the redirect has been completed, the diagram be given to the witness and he will withdraw to a secluded place and perhaps he could come back in order to make a comparison, because we have two graphical comparisons and the witness is saying it doesn't correspond. I don't know what that means when you say it doesn't correspond. For you it means something, Mr. Jankovic. I am not asking for an explanation now. We will have the witness come back so that he can criticise the diagram that he sees. All right. You want to continue, Mr. Nobilo, or have you completed what you wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first is the following. We saw Exhibit 565, it is the howitzer 122-millimetre D30J, and in one section it quotes the distance, a distance of 17.300 metres. You had some facts and figures contained in another document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 564, and it stated 17.133 metres. Now I would like to ask you the following: Regardless of the fact whether it is 17.133 range or 17.300 metres, would that vitally affect your findings as to the range of the howitzer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have the model with me, and I have my computer, I did the calculations last night, the other calculations, so that I could answer that question. I have the exact data now, with the new figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You sort of thought -- I don't understand. You had foreseen this question, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, since yesterday I said that it wouldn't change anything, so I prepared myself in order to defend what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it's diagram "F." The range would not be 15.141, but would have been 15 kilometres and 302 metres. For diagram "C," the angle of elevation would not be 30.1 degrees, but 29.4 degrees. And the angle of fall would not be 48.1, but 47.4. On diagram "D" the angle of elevation would not be 27.7 degrees, but 27.5 degrees. And the angle of fall remains the same, but the wind is not 13.5 but 11 metres. On the basis of these figures, I would repeat what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Tell us one more thing, please. According to your knowledge -- is it more precise, 17.133 metres, is that more precise, or the other figure published for commercial purposes, the 17.300 figure? Which figure is more exact, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not doubt that the source data is 17.133, since I said that that was an official document. The other was a secondary document, and it is the official documents that are the source of our information. I would also like to add an explanation. Very frequently it happens, and it even happened to us, it even happened to me, when we develop a weapon and we calculate the range, and we publish documentation in order to advertise the weapon, and we provide the data, and then afterwards, when the development has been completed, we don't quite have exactly what it is that we wanted. So, for example, I believe that in the same document, for this projectile it said that it had a 20-kilometre range, but our tests later on said that it was greater than 20 kilometres. It was 20 kilometres and 50 metres. So that does happen. It's because of this that the firing tables are the most important and most exact documents that exist. The book that I showed you must be in agreement with the firing tables, because this is also an official book as the tables are official. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now my last question. Any expert, but an expert of course, if any expert were to take these elements into consideration, the ones that you had, would he, by means of calculations, arrive at the same result as you yourself did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I will add only a few details that I haven't already said, and that is that I used the Russian aerodynamic coefficient of 1943, and I used the normal projectile, 122 explosive, figures because even in the text, it says that it was the projectile of the normal point, and everything I said is something that every specialist would also say according to calculations reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, counsel would have told you that we are not military experts in court and, therefore, we depend, to a great deal, on expert assistance from persons of your training and background. So do forgive me if I ask you a question or two which may appear to you to be elementary in nature. Let me first ask you this question: Is it the case that the trajectory of a shell need not have the same angle of elevation as the angle of fall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is never not the same. If they are the same elevation, the fall angle is always greater than the angle of elevation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would I be right in understanding you to mean this, that the angle of fall could indicate two things, namely, the range of the shell and the direction from which it came?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The direction -- more or less, yes. There is another effect which comes into play which is deviation, but that's not so important. It's one or two degrees. I wasn't even sure that one should really talk about it here because it's not important. It's not significant enough. But the angle of fall cannot tell you exactly what the angle of elevation is because the angle of fall influences not only the angle of elevation but ordinarily the initial velocity, and from the photographs that you've seen, you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, it may be that I have misled you. I wasn't asking whether the angle of fall would indicate the angle of elevation, but only whether the angle of fall would indicate the range of the shell and the direction from which it came.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Do bear with me, Professor. You are an expert and we are not. Now, I have heard mention before of Jane's publication, but I have to be frank with you, I don't think I've ever consulted it. What is the correct title of that publication; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Jane's, you're talking about Jane's publication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Jane's publication.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not the one who mentioned it. It was Mr. Cayley. I look at it. I'm familiar with it. It's a source of information, but it's not really scientific. It's got more of a commercial orientation. For a technical person, a scientific person, like myself and for my colleagues, that's not a source of much information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Again, I apologise to you, Professor, if I suggested that you had mentioned the publication to me, but you had discussed it, and so I was asking for its correct title. Would I be right in supposing that that publication has been going now for some time, perhaps, for some decades?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does the publication consist of advertisements of new weaponry or does it consist of assessments made by experts on the weaponry of various states?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said to you, it's not a publication that we, who work in the technical areas, are very interested in. I can tell you what I think about it, but that's simply my opinion, and I'm not sure that everything I'm going to say is right. I know that it is a company in Switzerland, I think, that produces it, and it is especially used for high military officials to see what can be bought, what possibilities exist, in respect of knowing what company or countries produce what. It's expensive. It's a big book. It's filled with information, interesting information for military people, especially for those people who are involved in logistics for the armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it a publication which is relied upon by military authorities worldwide?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the last area of interest to me concerns the testimony of witnesses about the shells which fell on Zenica. Would I be correct in recalling you as saying that the testimony of the witnesses which you read suggested that those shells were explosive shells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, does the fact that the shells were explosive shells tell you anything about the range of those shells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The firing tables, for instance, the one I have with me, there are the firing tables for projectiles, anti-tank, and in the same volume, there are explosive projectiles and then tables for illuminating shells and those also that leave smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you have different types of explosive shells such that some types extend over a longer range than other types?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I showed you that there were two explosive projectiles of different characteristics and different ranges, but in this table, there was only one. Now, there's the third that I constructed which has an even greater range. We don't have firing tables for that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have some questions, not questions of an expert, and I also apologise, as my colleague Judge Shahabuddeen did, for my lack of expertise. Should I understand that you found the evaluations of the witnesses in the statements that were given to you, that you found them somewhat superficial or am I wrong in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you explain what you mean by "superficial"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, in other words, not very rigorous.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you ever worked with NATO officers, western officers, to exchange your experiences, experiments, your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Your knowledge, in fact, which is quite great, was it ever made available to Croatia in the conflicts? Were you ever asked to put your knowledge on the side of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cooperated with the Croatian army from the very start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you able to draw up firing tables yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Should I understand that you refused to draw up the firing tables for this shell for which you said that there was no firing table?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that was not the problem. We didn't have the firing range. We didn't have instruments. Even if we had had a firing range, there was an embargo, and we could not get them, so we didn't have them. We didn't have the assets that we needed in order to do what would be needed in order to set up the firing tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is the first time in your statement that you're talking about instruments because I have to say that throughout your statement, you spoke only about the lack of a firing range. I have not been in the army for a long time, but I do remember that the firing ranges -- it seems to me that in a country like Croatia, won't you be able to find firing ranges? That's why I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm always afraid about going into too many details. Even when we talk about firing ranges, you have to make different types. There is one thing, the technical firing range, and then the other thing is those that can be used for units, but the technical firing ranges requires a great deal of instruments which are very expensive. You, first of all, have to make exact measurements for the impact points on all the coordinates. You have to measure the initial velocity, even the velocity along each point on the trajectory. You have to measure the atmosphere. You have to measure the wind and the temperature in respect of velocity, et cetera, temperature of the powder. There are many things and they have to be organised. In the former Yugoslavia, there were firing ranges but they were all on the Serbian side. Near Samac, there's a large firing range which is very well-equipped. There's another one on the coast. Well, it doesn't matter where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when did Croatia find itself with a firing range?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first one was, I'm not sure, but it was, at that time -- it didn't have instruments. The first ballistic one that we were able to set up was with the shell that I spoke to you about. That means at the beginning of 1997. At that point, we had the minimum necessary in order to set up the firing range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, Croatia was never able to procure the firing tables for those weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I do not have any other questions. We're going to take a break. We're going to ask you to do a little bit of work. Let me tell you the rules so that everything will be clear. This work will not give rise to any question, any question from the Defence or from the Prosecution. The witness will be a kind of an amicus curiae, further to Rule 70, I believe it is, that is, that he will come back to give us a short explanation, I hope, that is, of the criticism that he has of the charts that had been provided by Witness W. This will be put into the minutes. We're not going to go back to a polemic about what the witness said about this or that point. The Judges are asking for this additional information, so long as we're fortunate enough to have this expert with us. Now we're going to take a break. About how much time would you need, Mr. Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let me suggest something. We will give the interpreters a bit of a break. Let me suggest that we resume at 4.00. The witness will work, and if you agree, before we begin with the cross-examination of the previous witness, we will have Professor Jankovic speak to us once again, and we thank him for coming back. Is something wrong, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, not really a problem. I had a question for the Prosecutor. Does he want 524 through 526 to be tendered as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman doesn't agree, I suppose, about the video. I'm frightening Mr. Hayman now, I see. No, you don't have to be afraid. You know how to defend your interests. You hold the interests of your client very close to your heart, and we are very loyal to justice, but all of us are loyal here. I expressed what I wanted. I thought that the Prosecutor simply wanted to show the image of a gun. So you don't agree with the entire video or just the one point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The entire video. We don't know what the source is. It seems to us that it's made up of two clips. We also received information that these guns are shooting at Kiseljak, and the text says that Rajic is threatening Sarajevo. So there's quite a bit of confusion involved, and we couldn't even see the cannon properly, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, could you give us some clarification? I would like to have this little problem resolved. Of course, I could consult with my colleague to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, is there any objection to 564 and 565, which is a public document? These are extracts from Jane's 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No objections. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The video?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The video, I will find out exactly what the origin is and I will tell the Court. It hasn't been altered in any way. There's been no jiggery-pokery, as my learned friend suggests. It's simply an extract from Belgrade TV. We're most interested in the artillery piece. If my learned friend wishes, we can narrow it down and simply have the gun, which the witness couldn't identify anyway, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure this will reassure Mr. Hayman and Mr. Nobilo, if you were to cut up the video and do away with the interview part. I suppose that's possible, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm perfectly happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right. We can have a still of the video, if you like. We can make a still, starting with the video, but only the part showing the gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. You will give the Judges and the Defence the specific information. Does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We all agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Everybody is satisfied now, so we can take our break until 4.00. Is that all right, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. However, this document, the photograph, will be 567.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Professor. Thank you for having returned. So that things are very clear, the witness in this part of the testimony, we can say is the Tribunal's witness based on Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We are bringing him in as Rule 98 and it's a correction of -- having conferred with my colleague, we authorise each of the parties to make some comments, if they wish to. You had, Professor, the diagram, which was attached to the testimony of one of the witnesses. We don't have it with us, but it can be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO. The public can look at it. Now, you have an element about which you can make any comments that you consider appropriate to make, and the Tribunal thanks you for doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I redid the calculation and I compared the trajectory with the trajectory of the -- that is, we are not sure where we were in disagreement. There were two projectiles. I suppose it would be of interest to speak about the projectile that the Croatian army had, the OF 462, or would you like me to speak about both of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps both, since you studied both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then we need some more time. I only did it for one. For the second I would need more time. It would be too dangerous just to do it off the cuff. There could be mistakes. One needs to concentrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: About how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you would allow me the time that it would take for the other witness, I could make some preparations, and I could ask you exactly what it is that you are asking data for. I can tell you what the height is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What was the hypothesis of the witness who had spoken? What we are interested in is the contradiction that you see with the diagram. What is it? I don't really remember. What was it, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have everything in my head. He did not say what projectile was involved. It's because of that, that I was always speaking about two projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can make a comparison of the figures of the two projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be good. Can you assess about how much time you are going to need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About an hour. About an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. All right. We'll ask you to withdraw and we'll hear the next witness. Thank you. So that everything is clear, Professor Jankovic will come back at a time that we will set, at least an hour, and he will come to make his contribution to the diagram. In the meantime we will continue with the cross-examination of an unprotected witness and whose cross-examination has been postponed until today. I believe Mr. Harmon is going to do it and it's Mr. Tadic, the Minister of the Federation? Is that correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Judge Jorda, Judge Shahabuddeen and counsel. Yes, I will be conducting the cross-examination of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time, Professor Jankovic. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's too dangerous to do that quickly without a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you speak about danger so much, and you are an expert in explosives. That's what begins to worry us. All right. Wish you good work. We will now have Mr. Tadic brought in to the courtroom. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So that everything is clear, let me remind you that Mr. Tadic came yesterday. He is the former Minister of Justice of the Federation. As regards the procedural matters, the Trial Chamber decided that the cross-examination would be postponed until this afternoon. How long will this cross-examination take, Mr. Registrar, if you base it on the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: About two hours and 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Two hours and 10 minutes of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we start running late, 10 or 15 minutes late, could we work longer tonight, because Mr. Tadic was supposed to finish yesterday and then we asked him to stay for an extra day today, and he postponed some of the things he had to attend to. If we only reach about 10 to 15 minutes before the end of his statement, could we stay longer tonight so that he could finish tonight, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That depends upon how much time it takes, but we also take into account the interpreters. Ordinarily we should have another break. So I really don't know. That will depend upon the Prosecutor, who has the right to use two hours, and I suppose that he's not going to finish by then. Because, in addition to that we've got to hear the Professor again. All of you understood that once we speak about shells and trajectories, it takes a lot of time. Therefore, I don't think he will be able to leave tonight, unfortunately. Usher, please have the witness brought into the courtroom. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I really can't answer, Mr. Nobilo. It doesn't depend on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic. Thank you. Let me remind you that you are still under oath when you are asked questions. I'm very sorry, you may not be able to leave this evening, Mr. Tadic. I know that it's not pleasant for you, but we'll see. Maybe, but I have my doubts. Without wasting any more time, we'll give the floor to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My name is Mark Harmon and to my right is Andrew Cayley, and to his right is my other colleague Mr. Kehoe. Let me go directly to the examination. Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 22 placed on the ELMO, please. Mr. Tadic, there is a map that is to your left on the machine, we refer to as the ELMO, and in a moment, I hope, on the screen there will appear an image. Now, yesterday on direct examination you said that in 1993 you were in the Posavina, and you remained in the Posavina throughout 1993. I would ask you, please, to point out first of all the Posavina on this particular exhibit and then, secondly, you said you were in the Orasje area, or the Orasje pocket. Could you point out to the judges where is the Orasje pocket?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: This is the Posavina. I am indicating it right now. It is the Bosanska Posavina, the northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Orasje is here, approximately, where I showed it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You are pointing on the exhibit, above the letter "A" in the word Posavina, is the location of Orasje?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you are orienting us in this particular exhibit, would you point out the municipalities of Kiseljak, Vitez and Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: You see, this is where Vitez is, the place that I pointed to just now, and then Busovaca is over here, and then Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The territory that separated the Posavina from Vitez, Kiseljak and Busovaca municipalities was territory that was occupied by the Republika Srpska in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Most of this area was under occupation by the army of Republika Srpska. Part of it was also covered by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in the HVO in 1993, 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What position did you hold in the HVO, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to explain, in 1992, in April, on the 28th of April, I got out of Sarajevo and I reached Brcko. That is also Posavina. And, regrettably, I managed to spend only a single night in Brcko, and then I went out to the southwestern territory. We were there together, the Bosniaks, the Muslims and the Croats, and we set up a joint defence, that is to say it was called the 108th HVO Brigade, and it was also the civilian government that was formed too. I never had any posts in the army, but I was a member of the so-called Crisis Staff. That was a civilian element, a civilian component, and we operated as a government in wartime in an area that was not occupied yet. After Brcko, where I spent two or three months, I went to Bosanski Brod, which is also in Posavina, and after Bosanski Brod fell, I went to Orasje. In Orasje I was entrusted with the task of setting up civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you were in Orasje, were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Not in the sense of belonging to military units. I told you that I never belonged to the HVO in that sense. However, you must realise that as the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO came into existence, the same name covered both the civilian and the military components. The civilian component had its own separate part, in the sense of the executive and legislative and judiciary branches, whereas the military part had its own set-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A little bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Tadic, from your testimony that for a small portion of time, which you've told us about, you were a member of the military component of the HVO, then became a member of the other component of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: I never wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I take it, likewise, you were never a member of the military police of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to visit the Vitez, Kiseljak or Busovaca municipalities in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you visit those same municipalities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, in passing. As I was going from the south of the country towards the Posavina, towards the municipality of Brcko, the southwest part, which was under HVO units controlled, and these were joint forces at the time of Croats and Bosniaks, and as we were passing with convoys of food and logistics, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So I take it your answer is that you transited through one or all of those municipalities on a single occasion in 1992 on your way to the Posavina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: I went along the road that existed then. That is to say, that that road went through populated areas only in part, but most of it went over mountains, et cetera. So we managed to travel only where there weren't combat operations and where the situation permitted this to be done. So I travelled several times until the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified that when you arrived in the Orasje area, and I am quoting you from page 6 of your testimony of yesterday, lines 8 and on, that essentially in the entire year of 1993 your task was to set up the work of the courts and the Prosecutor's offices and the legal authorities and to set up civilian institutions of the parent authority from -- and I don't have the date here -- at the end of February or the beginning of March, 1994. So that was your responsibility while you were in Orasje area. My question to you, Mr. Tadic, is: Were you setting up these legal authorities and these civilian institutions for the authorities of Herceg-Bosna or for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to explain that I came to that area at the end of April, after I had established civilian authority in the territory of Brcko, together with others, and I already helped set up the military authorities, because I was the first one to write certain rules and regulations for the military police, but they were relevant only to the 100th Brigade of the HVO, Brcko, and then after that I went to Bosanski Brod. I think this was June or July, 1992. At that time the HVO council for Bosanska Posavina acted as an independent party and at that time I had the task of establishing civilian and military judiciary authorities in the territory of Bosanska Posavina. I elaborated the necessary acts and I took them to Zagreb, and part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your answer is very lengthy. I am limited in the amount of time I have, and my question was very specific to you. Were you setting up the courts and the prosecutors' offices for the authorities of Herceg-Bosna in 1993 or were you setting these authorities up for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was establishing these authorities for the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina; in 1993, within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In 1993, you were setting up those authorities for the authorities of Herceg-Bosna. My question to you then, Mr. Tadic, is, who directed you to do that in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of January, 1993, I was appointed assistant head of the justice department within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: -- and I was detached in Posavina, and my task there was to establish the judiciary. It hadn't been operating at all until then, and it hadn't been operating from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the assistance of the usher and have this exhibit marked as a Prosecutor's Exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I'm going to show you a document, and I'll give you a preview of it while it's being marked and before it's presented to you. This is from the Narodni list, and it indicates your appointment as the assistant head, and it indicates, and I'll let you take a look at this yourself, that this appointment went into effect on the 6th of January, 1993 and that you were appointed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic who was the president of the HVO Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to identify this in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 568.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me just very briefly ask you, when it's shown to you, to confirm that this is the decision announcing your appointment in the Narodni list.

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is a decision dated January 6, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your official title was what on this particular appointment?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
utterances.text: Assistant Head of the Department for Justice and Administration of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, thereafter, after you received this appointment, Mr. Tadic, you set about drafting various laws or various regulations dealing with the courts and dealing with civilian institutions of Herceg-Bosna, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MATO TADIC
